lesson.title: Lesson plan: {hub}
lesson.footer: Made with the Saving Planets Lesson Plan Builder. Free to copy and adapt for your class.

step.hookText: Share an Amazing Fact below and ask: what surprised you?
step.exploreText: Look at these solution pages together:
step.wrapText: Use the discussion questions, then the exit ticket.

questions: How does {sol} help both people and nature?
If you could ask the team behind {sol} one question, what would it be?

k3.label: K-3 (ages 5-8)
objectives: Name one way people help {hub} that is also good for nature.
Tell a friend one wow fact about {hub}.
Draw how people and animals both benefit.
materials: Screen or printouts of the solution page
k3.activity: Wow circle: read the fact aloud, then each child draws the helper (a person, an animal or a machine) and shares it.
k3.exit: Draw or say one way you could help {hub}.

g45.label: Grades 4-5
objectives: Describe a problem in {hub} and one solution that is working now.
Explain how the solution helps both people and nature.
Use two new vocabulary words correctly.
materials: Screens or printouts of the solution pages
Five W’s chart (who, what, when, where, why)
g45.activity: Solution detectives: in pairs, read one solution page and fill in the Five W’s, then share one surprise with the class.
g45.exit: Write one thing you learned and one question you still have.

g68.label: Grades 6-8
objectives: Compare two {hub} solutions: who runs them, what they do and where.
Support a claim with evidence from a cited source.
Explain the trade-offs of each solution for people and for nature.
materials: Screens or printouts of the solution pages
T-chart: benefits for people / benefits for nature
g68.activity: Compare and contrast: groups take two solution pages and build a T-chart of benefits for people and for nature, then rank which helps more and why.
g68.exit: Write a claim about {hub} and one piece of evidence that supports it.

g912.label: Grades 9-12
objectives: Evaluate the evidence behind a {hub} solution using its original sources.
Analyze how science, technology and policy combine in the solution.
Propose an improvement that benefits both people and nature.
materials: Source-evaluation checklist (who published it, when, what evidence)
g912.activity: Source check: groups trace one Amazing Fact to its original source, judge how strong the evidence is, and present a one-minute verdict.
g912.exit: In two sentences: which source was strongest, and why?

uni.label: University
objectives: Critically assess the published evidence for {hub} solutions and its limits.
Map the stakeholders, funding and governance behind one solution.
Design a monitoring or research question with measurable outcomes for people and nature.
materials: Devices with internet and library database access
Original reports and papers linked from each solution page
uni.activity: Seminar brief: each student writes a one-page brief on one solution: the evidence, the open questions, and how success could be measured for people and nature. Peer-review in pairs.
uni.exit: Submit one research question about {hub} and the data you would need to answer it.

Earth_Observation.html.name: Earth Observation
Earth_Observation.html.blurb: Satellites are like eyes in the sky. They watch forests, ice, air and oceans so we can protect them.

sols.d: JAXA's DAICHI-4 radar sees through clouds over a 200 km swath, continuing the radar record used for deforestation alerts.
ESA's Biomass satellite, launched April 29, 2025, carries the first P-band radar in space, seeing through forest canopies to measure the carbon stored in trees.
CHIME will image Earth in more than 200 colours of light to support sustainable farming, food security and biodiversity (ESA).
Europe's air monitoring service forecasts air pollution, smoke and dust worldwide twice a day for more than 23,500 users, free and open.

sols.t: Copernicus CO2M Carbon Dioxide Monitoring (ESA / EU)
sols.d: A planned trio of satellites that will measure the carbon dioxide and methane people release, so countries can check whether their emission cuts are working.

sols.t: Copernicus Emergency Management Service: On-Demand Mapping
sols.d: The European Union's emergency mapping service turns satellite images into maps for disaster teams, 24/7 since 2012, with more than 1,000 activations.
Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds, day and night, to map floods, earthquakes and ice; Sentinel-1C and 1D joined in 2024 and 2025.
Sentinel-2C joined the Copernicus fleet in September 2024, imaging land and coasts in 13 bands so forests and crops are checked every five days.
The Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellites measure Earth's oceans, land, ice and atmosphere, and a third satellite, Sentinel-3C, launched on September 15, 2026 (ESA).
From geostationary orbit on MTG-S1, Sentinel-4 measures air pollution such as nitrogen dioxide and ozone over Europe and North Africa every hour (ESA).
Copernicus Sentinel-5P maps the gases in the air we breathe, covering the whole planet every day with its Tropomi instrument (ESA).
Sentinel-6B, launched November 17, 2025, continues the precise record of global sea level that began in the early 1990s.
Digital Earth Africa turns satellite data into free and open maps of water, farmland and coasts for the whole African continent (Digital Earth Africa).
A camera photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day.
ESA–JAXA EarthCARE carries the first space cloud radar that can measure how cloud particles move up and down, sharpening forecasts of how clouds affect climate.
NASA's EMIT instrument on the International Space Station maps the minerals in desert dust and has spotted methane super-emitters from space (NASA JPL).
India's EOS-06, the third Oceansat, tracks ocean color, sea-surface temperature and winds; it imaged Cyclone Mandous and an algal bloom on day one.
Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat satellites are built to spot wildfires as small as 5 by 5 meters from space and get the data to firefighters fast.

sols.t: FIRMS Fire Information for Resource Management System (NASA)
sols.d: NASA's FIRMS delivers satellite fire detections within 3 hours anywhere on Earth, and in real time for the US and Canada. Free for firefighters and everyone.
Launched together on September 15, 2026, ESA's FLEX maps the faint glow of photosynthesis while Sentinel-3C watches oceans and land.
ESA's FORUM will measure Earth's outgoing far-infrared radiation, never measured from space before, filling a missing piece of the climate jigsaw (ESA).
Europe's Galileo is the world's most precise satellite navigation system, serving over five billion smartphone users and helping rescues (ESA).
Japan's SHIKISAI satellite checks the health of Earth from space every 2 or 3 days, tracking clouds, aerosols, ocean color, plants, snow and ice (JAXA).
NOAA's next generation of geostationary weather satellites, planned from 2032, will improve warnings of severe weather and hazards (NOAA).
JAXA's IBUKI GW tracks carbon dioxide, methane and nitrogen dioxide while also measuring the water cycle. Launched June 29, 2025 from Tanegashima Space Center.
Twin US-German satellites weigh Earth's water by measuring gravity, tracking groundwater, ice and sea level since 2018. Active.
JAXA's Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation maps rain around the world every hour, used by 18,673 registered users in 163 countries and regions.
ESA's first Scout mission uses reflected navigation-satellite signals to measure soil moisture, wetlands and frozen ground (ESA).
India's INSAT-3DS watches weather, land and oceans from geostationary orbit and carries a search-and-rescue transponder (ISRO).

sols.t: International Charter: Space and Major Disasters
sols.d: When disaster strikes, 17 space agencies and satellite operators pool their satellites and give free images to rescue teams. Activated 1,000 times.
NOAA's polar weather satellites circle Earth 14 times a day. Polar-orbiting satellites supply about 85% of the data used by weather prediction models.
Landsat 9 continues a 50-year record of Earth’s land, collecting 740 scenes a day and, with Landsat 8, seeing each place every 8 days.
Libera will measure how much energy leaves Earth each day, keeping a climate record that began in 2000 going strong (NOAA).
Three weather satellites now watch Europe and Africa from 36,000 km up, with new images every 2.5 minutes and a camera that catches lightning day and night.
The UN's satellite methane alert system has sent more than 3,500 alerts about major leaks in 33 countries, and responses rose from 1% to 12% in a year.
Launched August 2025 on Ariane 6, MetOp-SG-A1 carries Sentinel-5, which delivers daily global data on air pollutants, ozone and climate gases.
NISAR, a NASA and ISRO radar satellite launched from India on July 30, 2025, scans nearly all of Earth's land and ice twice every 12 days, even through clouds.
NASA's OCO-2 satellite has measured carbon dioxide around the planet since 2014, showing where carbon is released and where forests and oceans absorb it.
NASA's PACE reads the color of the ocean to track phytoplankton, the base of the marine food web, plus aerosols and clouds.
Three Canadian radar satellites watch Canada's land, coasts and Arctic day and night, through cloud and smoke, with about 250,000 images a year.
NOAA's SARSAT satellites relay distress beacon signals to rescuers; the international system has supported more than 50,000 rescues worldwide since 1982 (NOAA).
SMAP maps the water in Earth's soil from space, helping improve predictions of weather, floods and droughts (NASA).
SWOT measures more than 95% of Earth's lakes larger than 15 acres and rivers wider than 330 feet, the first global survey of fresh water.
Tanager-1, built by Planet with a NASA JPL-designed spectrometer for the nonprofit Carbon Mapper, pinpoints methane and CO2 plumes from single sources.
From geostationary orbit, NASA's TEMPO measures air pollution over North America every daylight hour, a first from space (NASA).
A worldwide science program where students and citizen scientists collect real environmental data: more than 293 million measurements from 127 countries.
Deep-ocean buoys, satellites, GPS signals and seafloor cables spot tsunamis in the open ocean so coastal communities get time to reach high ground (NOAA, NASA).

facts.x: CAMS draws on more than 80 satellite instruments plus ground measurements (CAMS).
facts.sn: CAMS, Introduction at the 8th General Assembly (June 12, 2024)

facts.x: A model of the CHIME instrument was put in a vacuum chamber and on a shaker to prove it can survive launch (ESA).
Three CO2M satellites will measure human-made carbon dioxide around the whole globe in about 3.5 days.
facts.sn: ESA, Europe’s carbon dioxide monitoring mission elevated to the power of three

facts.x: The mapping service has run 24/7 since 2012 without a single service disruption (Copernicus EMS).
Digital Earth Africa's Landsat-based maps of Africa start in 1984 (Digital Earth Africa).
EMIT collects more than 100,000 light spectra every second from the space station.
facts.sn: NASA JPL, Methane super-emitters mapped by EMIT

facts.x: EarthCARE carries the first cloud radar in space that can measure how fast cloud particles move up and down.
FIRMS combines fire detections from five satellites: Aqua, Terra, Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (NASA FIRMS).
facts.sn: NASA FIRMS, Fire Information for Resource Management System

facts.x: ESA calls the far-infrared a missing piece of the climate jigsaw that FORUM will fill in (ESA).
FireSat can detect a fire as small as 5 by 5 meters, about the footprint of two parking spaces.
facts.sn: Earth Fire Alliance, FireSat first light (Sep 16, 2026)

facts.x: SGLI observes light from near-ultraviolet to thermal infrared, from 380 nanometres to 12 micrometres (JAXA).
55,871 educators take part in GLOBE (GLOBE figures, October 16, 2026).
GSMaP maps rainfall for the whole globe every hour (JAXA).
facts.sn: JAXA EORC, GSMaP talk at IPWG-12 (July 2026)

facts.x: Each Galileo satellite's hydrogen maser clock keeps time to within 0.45 billionths of a second over 12 hours (ESA).
The Inspector General made six recommendations to reduce the risk of a gap in geostationary weather data and improve risk management (OIG).
facts.sn: U.S. Department of Commerce OIG, Evaluation of NOAA's Progress Implementing the GeoXO Satellite Program (OIG-26-009-I)

facts.x: Each HydroGNSS satellite weighs about 75 kilograms and measures 45 by 45 by 70 centimeters.
INSAT-3DS had a lift-off mass of 2,275 kg and is built on ISRO's I-2k bus (Ministry of Earth Sciences).
facts.sn: Press Information Bureau (Ministry of Earth Sciences), INSAT-3DS launch

facts.x: The Charter has been activated 1,000 times in 25 years, an average of about 40 activations a year (International Charter).

JPSS satellites orbit The curved path an object takes as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like a satellite circling Earth. Glossary pole to pole 14 times a day, covering the whole globe twice daily (NOAA).
facts.sn: NOAA NESDIS, Joint Polar Satellite System

facts.x: Libera is named for the daughter of Ceres in Roman mythology, a nod to the CERES instruments before it.
Around the world there are over three million lightning flashes every day (ESA).
OCO-2 makes around 100,000 measurements of Earth's carbon dioxide every day.
facts.sn: Caltech, NASA selects Caltech to operate the OCO missions (Aug 24, 2026)

facts.x: In ship detection mode, RCM can detect ships 25 m long across all waters within 2,000 km of Canada's coasts, every day (Canadian Space Agency).
facts.sn: Canadian Space Agency, RADARSAT Constellation Mission FAQ

facts.x: Satellites listening for emergency beacons helped rescue 300 people in and around the U.S. in 2025.
facts.sn: NOAA, NOAA satellites helped rescue 300 people in 2025

facts.x: SMAP's 20-foot (6-meter) "golden lasso" antenna is the largest rotating mesh antenna ever deployed in space (NASA JPL).
NASA–CNES SWOT keeps watch on the water levels of more than a million lakes larger than 15 acres.
Sentinel-3's temperature radiometer has two channels built just for spotting fires.
Sentinel-4 watches Europe's air pollution every hour from 36,000 km up.
facts.sn: ESA, Sentinel-4 offers first glimpses of air pollutants

facts.x: Sentinel-5P's Tropomi instrument sees a strip of Earth 2,600 kilometers wide in one pass.
NASA's TEMPO checks North America's air pollution every daylight hour from 22,000 miles up.
About 70 minutes after the 2025 Kamchatka earthquake, the SWOT satellite measured the tsunami from space: a wave more than 1.5 feet high racing across the Pacific.
facts.sn: NASA, SWOT satellite measures tsunami after massive quake

facts.x: In one year, the share of MARS alerts that got a response rose from 1% to 12% (UNEP).
facts.sn: UNEP press release, Better data driving action on methane emissions

terms.d: A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for the echoes. From space it can see the ground through clouds, day or night.
The curved path an object takes as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like a satellite circling Earth.
A greenhouse gas that traps much more heat than carbon dioxide over a few decades. It leaks from oil and gas sites, landfills and farms.
A series of giant ocean waves, usually caused by an undersea earthquake, volcano or landslide.
The total amount of living material, like the wood and leaves in a forest. Measuring it shows how much carbon plants store.
A kind of light our eyes can't see that we feel as heat. Special cameras use it to see warm objects and gases.
A gas high in the sky that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. Near the ground, ozone is a pollutant.
A gas, like carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in the air around Earth, the way a greenhouse keeps plants warm.
Tiny bits of dust, smoke, salt or pollution floating in the air. They can block sunlight and help clouds form.
A high orbit, about 22,000 miles up, where a satellite moves with Earth's spin and stays over the same spot.
A community of living things and the place they live, like a reef or a forest, all depending on each other.
Tiny plant-like living things that drift in water and use sunlight to make food. They make much of the oxygen we breathe and feed ocean life.

Deforestation.html.name: Forests
Deforestation.html.blurb: Forests are homes for animals and help keep our air clean. People are planting trees and protecting wild places.

sols.d: African Parks manages 24 protected areas in 13 countries, covering over 20 million hectares, in partnership with governments and local communities (nonprofit).
Since 1875, American Forests has worked to restore U.S. forests, from big natural landscapes to city streets, with more than 63 million trees planted.
Since 1972, the Arbor Day Foundation says it has planted more than half a billion trees, working in more than 60 countries (nonprofit figures).

sols.t: Costa Rica Payments for Environmental Services (FONAFIFO)
sols.d: Costa Rica's FONAFIFO pays the owners of forests and forest plantations for the environmental services they provide, under Forestry Law 7575 (FONAFIFO).
Eden: People+Planet restores landscapes with local communities, including a 394,000-hectare project in Tanzania's Rubeho Mountains (Eden).
Europe's wildfire system forecasts fire danger and maps burnt areas from satellites. In 2024 it mapped wildfires in 42 countries.
By thinning small trees, forest elephants help central Africa's rainforests store more carbon: 26 to 60 more tonnes of biomass per hectare (Nature Geoscience).
Galápagos Conservancy and the Galápagos National Park Directorate rear giant tortoises in breeding centres and return them to their home islands.
GEDI fires lasers from the International Space Station to measure the height and 3D shape of Earth's forests (University of Maryland).
Free satellite forest data and deforestation alerts from WRI; where Indigenous forest monitors used it, deforestation fell 52% in one year.
An African-led effort to restore land across the Sahel. A 2020 UN status report counted about 4 million hectares restored inside the Great Green Wall zone.
With farmers and pastoralists in Africa, Justdiggit is restoring 525,000 hectares of dry land and has brought back 32.3 million trees (organization figures).
Life Terra and its partners have planted more than 36 million trees across Europe (company figure), working toward a goal of 500 million trees.
Near-real-time monitoring that finds urgent deforestation, identifies its causes and publishes easy-to-read reports.
About 80 species of mangrove trees guard tropical coastlines: their tangled roots hold mud in place, soften storm surges and give fish food and shelter.
Since 2014, One Tree Planted has planted more than 171 million trees with 489 partners in 84 countries (organization figure).
Started by a 9-year-old in 2007, Plant-for-the-Planet trains young Climate Justice Ambassadors and restores forests, including Mexico's Mayan forests.
A goal, a movement and a government-funded programme to eradicate the most harmful introduced predators.
Solar-powered Guardian listening devices and SI detect chainsaws in real time; Rainforest Connection reports more than 726,000 hectares of rainforest protected.
Rewilding Europe helps wild nature come back across Europe. Rewilding Europe, working with local partners in large pioneering landscapes.
Every year about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust falls on the Amazon, delivering some 22,000 tons of phosphorus that the rainforest needs (NASA).
Terraformation grows native, biodiverse forests from seed to canopy across the tropics and Hawaii, funding seed collection, nurseries, planting and monitoring.

sols.t: The Amazon Makes Its Own Rainy Season
sols.d: Water breathed out by Amazon trees starts the rainy season two to three months before winds alone would bring it (NASA JPL).

sols.t: Three Trees for Every One Removed
sols.d: Saving Planets' own forest rule: plant three trees for every one removed, so each removal becomes a net gain for habitat, soil and shade, and is easy to verify.
Partnering with East African farmers on regenerative farms: 450M+ trees grown and 99,000 acres restored (nonprofit figures).
WeForest has grown more than 118 million trees and has 100,000 hectares of forest under restoration and conservation (WeForest).
Gray wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 after nearly 70 years; in January 2026 at least 84 lived in the park, in eight packs (NPS).

facts.x: Of the 37 species African Parks has moved, 18 had disappeared from the area before they were brought back (nonprofit figures).
Amazon trees start their own rainy season two to three months before the ocean-driven rains arrive.
facts.sn: NASA JPL, the Amazon makes its own rainy season

facts.x: American Forests was founded in 1875, making it more than 150 years old.
The Foundation works with more than 5,400 planting partners who work locally (Arbor Day Foundation).
Funding first came from one third of the fuel consumption tax, and now 3.5% of the single fuel tax goes to the programme (FONAFIFO).
Since 2018, Sentinel-2 images let EFFIS map fires under 30 hectares; it now maps about 95% of the area that burns in the EU each year (EFFIS).
In Tanzania's Rubeho Mountains, 92,458 people across 40 villages are helping restore 394,000 hectares of land.
The extinction of forest elephants would cut aboveground biomass in central African rainforests by 7% (Nature Geoscience).
Each GEDI laser spot on the ground is 25 meters wide, and spots are 60 meters apart.
facts.sn: University of Maryland, GEDI mission overview

facts.x: In June 2020 the 15 original Española adults were released back on their island, ending one of the most successful breeding programmes in the world (Galápagos Conservancy).
facts.sn: Galápagos Conservancy, Española tortoises return home

facts.x: Where Indigenous monitors used Global Forest Watch data, deforestation fell 52% in a year.
facts.sn: Global Forest Watch (now Global Nature Watch), Our History

facts.x: African countries are working to restore a band of land across the Sahel, south of the Sahara.
facts.sn: UNCCD, First Great Green Wall status report

facts.x: Justdiggit digs smile-shaped pits that catch rain and turn dry land green.
MAAP has documented causes of deforestation including gold mining, oil palm, cacao, small-scale agriculture, logging roads and hydroelectric dams (Amazon Conservation).
There are about 80 species of mangrove trees, and their tangled roots help shield coastlines from storm surges.
facts.sn: NOAA, What is a mangrove forest?

facts.x: One Tree Planted and its partners have planted more than 171 million trees in 84 countries.
More than 100,000 children and youth in 76 countries have become Climate Justice Ambassadors.
The aim is to remove every last animal and stop them from coming back, which is much harder than keeping numbers down (DOC).
Rainforest Connection hides solar-powered listening devices in trees to hear illegal logging as it happens.
Wild European bison, Europe's largest land mammal, grew from about 2,500 to 7,000 in 10 years.
About 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust fall on the Amazon each year, enough to fill 104,908 semi trucks.
facts.sn: NASA, Saharan dust feeds the Amazon

facts.x: WeForest has engaged 45,000 households in alternative livelihood activities.
Recorders placed around the park capture wolf howls, helping estimate wolf numbers in remote areas (NPS).
facts.sn: National Park Service, Wolf management in Yellowstone

terms.d: A tree that grows in salty water along tropical coasts. Its tangled roots protect shores from waves and shelter young fish.
The variety of all living things in a place: plants, animals, fungi and tiny microbes.
The total amount of living material, like the wood and leaves in a forest. Measuring it shows how much carbon plants store.
A community of living things and the place they live, like a reef or a forest, all depending on each other.
Planting trees where a forest was lost so it can grow back.
Large brown seaweed that grows in cool ocean water and forms underwater forests full of sea life.
A coastal wetland of grasses that floods with salty tide water. It soaks up storm surges and stores carbon in its mud.
A gas, like carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in the air around Earth, the way a greenhouse keeps plants warm.
A greenhouse gas that traps much more heat than carbon dioxide over a few decades. It leaks from oil and gas sites, landfills and farms.
A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for the echoes. From space it can see the ground through clouds, day or night.

Lakes.html.name: Lakes
Lakes.html.blurb: Lakes hold fresh water for animals and people. Divers and robots are pulling trash out of them.

sols.d: Each year, Adopt-a-Beach volunteers remove tens of thousands of pounds of litter from Great Lakes beaches, about 85% of it plastic.
Clean Lakes Alliance works to improve water quality in Madison's Yahara lakes; it reports 81 monitoring stations and over $1.4 million in grants (its figures).
Clean Up the Lake removes submerged litter from freshwater lakes using scuba divers and volunteers, and GPS-pins, sorts and weighs every piece it finds.
The Great Lakes Plastic Cleanup captures plastic across the world's largest freshwater system using Seabins, drones, and beach robots.

sols.t: Keep Tahoe Blue (League to Save Lake Tahoe)
sols.d: Keep Tahoe Blue, the League to Save Lake Tahoe, has protected the lake for decades, and its volunteers picked up 1,330 pounds of litter after July 4, 2026.

sols.t: Lake Erie Harmful Algal Bloom Forecast (NOAA)
sols.d: NOAA forecasts and tracks toxic algae in western Lake Erie through the summer so cities and swimmers can keep drinking water and people safe (NOAA NCCOS).
Saving Planets' own lake solution: recover plastic from freshwater lakes by skimming, shoreline collection and divers, before it travels downstream to the sea.
Since 1998, the Global Nature Fund's Living Lakes Network has protected and restored lakes and wetlands with 130 member organizations in more than 60 countries.
A Nevada nonprofit whose ROVs and volunteer divers pull submerged trash from Lake Tahoe, from the surface down to 1,640 feet: over 13 tons in summer 2024 alone.

facts.x: About 85% of the litter Adopt-a-Beach volunteers pick up on Great Lakes beaches is plastic.
facts.sn: Alliance for the Great Lakes, Adopt-a-Beach

facts.x: Volunteer monitors post lake conditions to the LakeForecast app, warning when potentially toxic algae blooms form (Clean Lakes Alliance).
Every year after the Fourth of July, Tahoe volunteers clean up the beaches. 2026 was the 13th year.
facts.sn: Keep Tahoe Blue, Red, White & Blue Cleanup 2026

facts.x: NOAA forecasts toxic algae on Lake Erie the way meteorologists forecast storms.
facts.sn: NOAA NCCOS, Timely toxin data helped Ohio deliver safe drinking water

facts.x: Living Lakes helps protect Lake Hovsgol, a lake about 2 million years old, and the nomadic families who live beside it.

terms.d: When tiny water plants called algae grow out of control. Some make toxins that can harm people, pets and fish.
A community of living things and the place they live, like a reef or a forest, all depending on each other.
Pieces of plastic smaller than 5 millimeters, about the size of a grain of rice or smaller. They come from bigger plastic breaking apart.
The variety of all living things in a place: plants, animals, fungi and tiny microbes.
All the land where rain and snow drain into the same river or lake.

Oceans.html.name: Oceans
Oceans.html.blurb: The ocean covers most of our planet. People are cleaning up plastic and growing sea gardens so fish, turtles and people all stay healthy.

sols.d: 4ocean removes plastic from oceans, rivers, and coastlines with full-time cleanup crews, funded by products made from recovered plastic.
The Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi tracks more than 18.5 million mangroves planted across over 1,775 hectares with its new Mangrove Observatory.
Close to 4,000 robotic floats dive through the ocean and send back temperature and salinity data, free to everyone. The 3 millionth profile came in 2024.
A satellite system that tracks wildlife and ocean instruments from tiny transmitters, following more than 8,000 animals every month for conservation science.
A New York nonprofit restoring the harbor with oyster reefs, aiming for one billion oysters by 2030 (nonprofit figures).
Free, open ocean data and forecasts for the whole planet. In 2025 users downloaded almost 15,000 terabytes of ocean data from Copernicus Marine.
Coral Gardeners grows corals in nurseries and replants them on reefs in French Polynesia, Fiji and Thailand: 238,250 corals planted so far.
Researchers capture coral spawn and rear millions of baby corals for damaged reefs; the first Coral IVF corals reproduced on the Great Barrier Reef in 2021.
NOAA's Coral Reef Watch uses satellites to warn of the ocean heat that bleaches corals, with daily monitoring of 95% of the world's coral reefs.
Coral Restoration Foundation had returned 253,833 corals to Florida's reefs by the end of 2024 (organization figure). Florida's Coral Reef in the Florida Keys.
Coral Vita grows reef-building corals on land up to 50 times faster than in nature, and says it has grown over 100,000 corals (company figures).
Global Fishing Watch uses satellites and SI to map fishing; its 2024 Nature study found about 75% of industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked.
Since 1985, Heal the Bay has worked to make the coastal waters and watersheds of Greater Los Angeles safe, healthy and clean (Heal the Bay).
Volunteer divers recover ghost nets: Healthy Seas reports 1,309.1 tons of nets and marine litter removed since 2013 (Healthy Seas figure).
Since 1986, more than 19 million volunteers have collected more than 400 million pounds of trash from beaches and waterways (Ocean Conservancy).
Kelp can grow up to 18 inches a day, building underwater forests that feed and shelter thousands of species. Nature, studied and protected by NOAA and partners.
The MAR Insurance Programme, run by the nonprofit MAR Fund, uses parametric insurance to pay for fast reef repair after hurricanes along the 1,000 km Mesoamerican Reef.
Founded by ocean scientist Dr. Sylvia Earle, Mission Blue backs a community-led network of 168 Hope Spots, ocean places local champions work to protect.
Mote scientists have restored more than 216,000 corals to Florida's Coral Reef, and their restored corals now spawn (Mote figure).
A sailing nonprofit that has pulled more than 850,000 pounds of plastic from the Pacific Gyre in 10 voyages (nonprofit figure).
The Palau National Marine Sanctuary makes about 80% of Palau's exclusive economic zone a no-take area, with the other 20% kept as a Domestic Fishing Zone.
Designated in 2025 as America's 18th national marine sanctuary, Papahānaumokuākea covers 582,570 square miles of Pacific Ocean around Hawaiʻi (NOAA).
Tiny ocean plants produce about half of Earth's oxygen, making phytoplankton one of the planet's most important natural systems.
Plastic Bank pays collectors in vulnerable communities to gather ocean-bound plastic, exchanged at local branches for income, food vouchers and school supplies.
Plastic Odyssey sets up small recycling factories in places with no recycling system, turning plastic waste into useful products and local jobs.
The Mediterranean seagrass Posidonia oceanica forms meadows that are thousands of years old and store carbon in the seafloor (CEAB-CSIC).
Project Seagrass, a UK charity, has planted more than 150,000 seagrass seeds to bring back underwater meadows (organization figures).
Salt marshes are nurseries for more than 75% of fisheries species and buffer shorelines from erosion and floods (NOAA). Twice a day with the tides, all year.
Sea Turtle Conservancy works in 8 countries, has tagged and monitored more than 550 turtles and trained over 1,200 researchers (nonprofit figures).
Seabin's floating bins have captured 33.0 million items in Sydney Harbour since 2020, including 18.9 million microplastics (company figures).
Seagrass covers just 0.1% of the seafloor but stores 11% of the ocean's buried organic carbon, and one acre can support almost 40,000 fish, NOAA says.
SeaTrees connects people with local partners restoring mangroves, coral reefs, kelp forests and seagrass meadows around the world (SeaTrees).
Surfrider Foundation volunteers protect the ocean, waves and beaches, and in 2025 they removed 338,383 pounds of trash from U.S. coasts (Surfrider).
The Ocean Cleanup removes legacy plastic from ocean garbage patches and intercepts it in rivers: more than 65 million kilograms caught as of October 2026.

Planetary_Defense.html.name: Planetary Defense
Planetary_Defense.html.blurb: Scientists watch the sky for space rocks. A NASA spacecraft called DART even nudged an asteroid to show we can move one!

sols.t: ATLAS Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System
sols.d: Four robotic telescopes, two in Hawaiʻi, search the entire dark sky every 24 hours for asteroids that could hit Earth, so people can be warned.
A NASA-funded survey in Arizona that has discovered more near-Earth objects than any other: 17,918 near-Earth asteroids since 1995.
Three spacecraft will wait in space for a fresh comet and fly past it together to make a 3D map; launch is planned for late 2028 or early 2029 (ESA).
On 5 July 2026, JAXA's Hayabusa2 passed about 400 m above asteroid Torifune, the closest flyby of any Solar System body so far (JAXA).
ESA's Hera arrives at the asteroid Dimorphos in November 2026 to measure what NASA's DART impact did, turning deflection into a repeatable defense.
NASA's Lucy is touring asteroids; after Dinkinesh and Donaldjohanson, it reaches its first Trojan asteroid, Eurybates, on 11 August 2027 (NASA).
Europe's asteroid watch centre computes orbits and impact risks every day and keeps a public list of every asteroid with a non-zero chance of hitting Earth.
NASA NEO Surveyor is the first space telescope built to find hazardous asteroids, including dark ones hidden in the Sun's glare. Launch NET September 2027.
On April 13, 2029, asteroid Apophis passes about 20,000 miles from Earth. NASA's OSIRIS-APEX meets it in June 2029 to see how that close pass changes it.
Two telescopes on Haleakalā, Maui, that in 2021 found nearly as many near-Earth objects as the rest of the world's observatories combined.
ESA and JAXA's Ramses must launch by spring 2028 to meet Apophis before its 2029 Earth pass. Its €81.2 million build contract was signed in February 2026.
How the James Webb Space Telescope tracked asteroid 2024 YR4 in February 2026 and ruled out a 2032 Moon impact, two years before ground telescopes could.

Polar.html.name: Polar
Polar.html.blurb: The poles are covered in ice. Satellites measure the ice from space, so we can see how it is changing.

Two Copernicus satellites will measure sea ice, sea-surface temperature and salinity over 95% of the globe every day, with sub-daily polar views (ESA).

sols.t: CRISTAL Polar Ice and Snow Altimeter (ESA)
sols.d: CRISTAL will carry the first dual-frequency radar altimeter to measure polar sea-ice thickness and the snow on top, following ESA's CryoSat (ESA).
CryoSat measures polar sea ice and the great ice sheets from space, and its data revealed 85 hidden lakes under Antarctica (ESA).
NASA's ICESat-2 laser fires 10,000 pulses a second to measure ice sheets, sea ice, forests and coastal seafloor in 3D. Active.
About 100 scientists from the UK, US, South Korea, Germany and Sweden are working out how fast Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier could raise sea levels (ITGC).
Two shoebox-size NASA satellites measure the far-infrared heat that Earth's poles send into space (NASA JPL). Last reviewed: October 2026 · 4 sources cited
The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores backup copies of the world's crop seeds free of charge, more than 100 metres inside an Arctic mountain (Seed Vault).

Project-Rawane.html.name: Project Rawane
Project-Rawane.html.blurb: Earth and space help each other. Taking care of one helps take care of the other.

sols.d: ESA's Ariel will study the atmospheres of a thousand planets orbiting other stars, revealing what they are made of (ESA).
NASA's Artemis program: Artemis I flew in 2022, Artemis II carried four astronauts 252,756 miles from Earth in April 2026, and Artemis III is targeted for 2027.
After eight years in space, BepiColombo enters orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026, the first mission to put two spacecraft there (ESA).
NASA's Dragonfly is a car-size rotorcraft that will fly across Saturn's moon Titan to study the chemistry that came before life (NASA).
ESA's EnVision will study Venus from its inner core to its upper atmosphere, and may show how a planet like ours got so hot. Launch is planned for late 2031.
NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will study how the solar wind strips Mars' atmosphere, after an Earth slingshot in fall 2026.
Europe's first Mars rover, Rosalind Franklin, will drill 2 meters down to look for signs of past life, targeting launch in 2028.

NASA's Veggie garden grows fresh food on the International Space Station; in 2015 astronauts ate the first lettuce grown in it (NASA).

Rivers.html.name: Rivers
Rivers.html.blurb: Rivers carry water from the land to the sea. Trash catchers and dam removals help fish swim home again.

In Oregon's Bridge Creek, beavers given simple dam starters raised juvenile steelhead survival 52% and production 175% (NOAA Fisheries).
Seoul removed an ageing road and elevated motorway that covered the Cheonggyecheon stream and restored it along a 5.84 km corridor through the city centre.
Since 1966, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation has worked to save the Bay and its rivers, adding more than 21 million oysters in fiscal year 2026 (CBF).
Two Elwha River dams came down between 2011 and 2014, and more than 20 million tons of trapped sediment flowed downstream to rebuild the river and coast.
FreshWater Watch trains citizen scientists to test rivers, lakes and ponds: 80,000+ datasets from 22,000+ volunteers (organization figures).
Free global river flood forecasts up to 30 days ahead, plus 4-month outlooks, from the Copernicus Emergency Management Service.

Four Klamath River dams came out by October 2024, reopening more than 400 miles of habitat to salmon, steelhead and lamprey (Klamath River Renewal).
A barge-based river cleanup crew that, with more than 141,000 volunteers, has pulled over 14 million pounds of trash from U.S. rivers.

Baltimore's Trash Wheels intercept about 500 tons of trash a year before it reaches the harbor and the Chesapeake Bay (organization figure).

Free satellite data on how much water crops and land use, now for all 48 contiguous states, with more than 13,000 registered users.

The Great Bubble Barrier's bubble curtain guides plastic out of Amsterdam's canals into a catchment across the full width and depth, while boats and fish pass.
Trout Unlimited restores and reconnects cold, clean rivers, reconnecting 1,052 miles of streams in its 2024-25 season (Trout Unlimited).
Waterkeeper Alliance unites hundreds of local Waterkeeper groups that patrol and protect more than 6 million square miles of rivers, lakes and coastlines.

Gaganyaan G1, ISRO's first uncrewed Gaganyaan flight, is targeted for late 2026 on the human-rated HLVM3 rocket (ISRO).

Atmospheric drag is Earth's natural space debris removal: it pulls low-orbit junk down to burn up, faster when the Sun is active, but barely works up high.

ESA's Juice will study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa, with 35 moon flybys after it reaches Jupiter in July 2031. Cruising.

LignoSat, the world's first wooden satellite, proved wood can survive in orbit; a follow-on is a potential solution on the horizon.

The first Otter launched October 1, 2026 for NASA's SSPICY mission, inspecting up to four dead satellites and rocket bodies from 2027.
Saving moons, saving planets: the Moon keeps Earth's 23.5-degree tilt in check, which keeps our seasons and climate stable (NASA).
Titan is a prebiotic time capsule, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft explores it from 2034, building radar, power and autonomy tools that matter for Earth.
NASA selected SpaceX to build the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle that will guide the International Space Station safely out of orbit after 2030.
The Zero Debris Charter sets shared targets to stop creating space debris by 2030; by May 2026 it had 228 signatories from 34 countries (ESA).

The total amount of living material, like the wood and leaves in a forest. Measuring it shows how much carbon plants store.
A gas, like carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in the air around Earth, the way a greenhouse keeps plants warm.
A kind of light our eyes can't see that we feel as heat. Special cameras use it to see warm objects and gases.

Space_Weather.html.name: Space Weather & Shields
Space_Weather.html.blurb: The Sun sends out storms of energy. Earth has invisible shields, and satellites warn us when a storm is coming.

sols.d: Aditya-L1 is ISRO's first space-based solar observatory, studying the Sun from a halo orbit around L1, about 1.5 million km from Earth.
The first mission dedicated to Earth's exosphere, Carruthers watches our planet's ultraviolet halo from about a million miles sunward.
NOAA's GOES-19 carries CCOR-1, the world's first operational space-based coronagraph, imaging the Sun's corona every 15 minutes.
NASA's IMAP watches the Sun from about a million miles sunward and can give about a half hour's warning of incoming radiation.
The first spacecraft to fly through the Sun's outer atmosphere, helping scientists understand the space weather that affects life and technology on Earth.
Four suitcase-sized NASA satellites image the Sun's corona and solar wind together, in 3D, since March 2025. Active in low Earth orbit.

sols.t: SOHO Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (ESA / NASA)
sols.d: Watching the Sun nonstop since 1995, SOHO helps experts predict solar storms and has found more than 5,000 comets (NASA).
ESA and NASA's Solar Orbiter took the first close-up images of the Sun's poles, coming within 42 million km of the Sun. Active, orbiting the Sun.
NOAA's SOLAR-1 (formerly SWFO-L1) watches the Sun from L1, about one million miles from Earth, streaming space weather data to forecasters in real time.
Three natural shields protect Earth: the heliosphere, the magnetosphere, and the atmosphere with its ozone layer, deflecting solar wind and most harmful UV-B.
NASA's twin TRACERS satellites fly through Earth's polar cusps to study magnetic reconnection, a key driver of space weather.
ESA's Vigil will watch the Sun from L5, giving up to four to five days' notice of certain space weather effects. Launch is planned for 2031.

facts.x: Earth wears a faint ultraviolet halo, the geocorona, first photographed from the Moon by Apollo 16 in 1972; NASA's Carruthers mission now charts it from a million miles away.
GOES-19's CCOR-1 is the world's first operational space-based coronagraph, imaging the Sun's faint corona every 15 minutes.
From about a million miles toward the Sun, NASA's IMAP can give astronauts and spacecraft near Earth about a half hour's warning of incoming radiation.
Parker's 4.5-inch-thick carbon-composite shield can withstand temperatures of nearly 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit (1,377 Celsius).

In 1998 contact with SOHO was lost for weeks. A powerful radar A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for the echoes. From space it can see the ground through clouds, day or night. Glossary signal from Earth found it, and engineers brought it back to work (ESA).

terms.d: A steady stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun in every direction.
The curved path an object takes as it travels around a planet, moon or star, like a satellite circling Earth.
A gas high in the sky that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun. Near the ground, ozone is a pollutant.
Earth's invisible magnetic shield. It steers most of the Sun's charged particles away from our planet.
A spot in space where the pull of the Sun and Earth balance, so a spacecraft can stay in place with little fuel. L1 sits between Earth and the Sun.
An instrument that collects light (or other energy) to see faraway things more clearly.
A high orbit, about 22,000 miles up, where a satellite moves with Earth's spin and stays over the same spot.
An asteroid or comet whose orbit brings it close to Earth's path around the Sun. Scientists track them to make sure none is on course to hit us.
A tool that sends out radio waves and listens for the echoes. From space it can see the ground through clouds, day or night.
